USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture and Huawei Entity List pressure without further escalation. Signal willingness to negotiate at the upcoming G20 Osaka summit (late June) but concede nothing while China has backtracked on its commitments. Do not yet trigger the remaining ~$300B tariff tranche — that weapon is more valuable as a credible threat than as a fired round, given the direct hit to US consumers it would represent.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is real but asymmetric — we hold more leverage than China, yet the costs are mounting. On the threat side: $1.1 trillion in S&P 500 market value has been erased since May 5 (CNBC, May 13). The 10-year Treasury yield has collapsed from 3.06% (Nov 2018) to 2.37% (May 15), a 69bp flight-to-safety that signals genuine growth anxiety (country_health, DGS10). The yield curve is dangerously flat — 2Y at 2.16%, 10Y at 2.37 — flashing recession warning signals. Tariffs are fully passed through to US importers, costing the average household $300-$800/year (Econofact, May 14), and the White House has already spent $12B on farmer bailouts (Guardian, May 13). Soybean prices hit 10-year lows. If we extend 25% tariffs to the remaining $300B of Chinese imports, the cost disproportionately hits consumer products like iPhones, directly threatening the consumption-driven US economy (CNBC/FTSE Russell, May 13).

However, the leverage calculus favors us. China backtracked on nearly all aspects of the draft deal — deleting commitments on IP, forced tech transfer, competition policy, financial services, and currency (Reuters, May 8). This gave us legitimate cause to escalate. Our Huawei Entity List action (May 15) is a precision weapon: Huawei depends on US suppliers (Qualcomm, Intel, Google Android) and this threatens to cripple China's premier tech champion. China's retaliation capacity is constrained by the trade imbalance — they can only target $60B of our goods vs. our $250B coverage. China's economy faces 0.5-1 percentage point GDP drag if this escalates further (Morgan Stanley, via WaPo, May 13). Consumer sentiment remains strong at 100 (UMCSENT, May), the dollar is stable at ~115.9 (DTWEXBGS), and the Fed has room to cut if needed (Fed Funds at 2.39%).

The action score of -0.1 reflects a hold posture with a slight hawkish tilt. We should maintain all existing pressure — the 25% tariffs on $250B and the Huawei Entity List — but pause before firing the $300B tranche. The G20 in Osaka provides a natural off-ramp if China returns to the table with real concessions on enforcement. The worst outcome is triggering consumer-facing tariffs that tip us into recession while China digs in; the best is that Huawei pressure and existing tariff pain bring Beijing back with binding enforcement language. Hold the line.
key_factors: $1.1 trillion in stock market value lost since May 5 tariff threat
10Y Treasury yield collapsed 69bp to 2.37% — flight to safety and recession signal
China backtracked on nearly all aspects of draft trade deal (Reuters exclusive)
Huawei Entity List placement (May 15) — powerful leverage over China's tech champion
Tariffs fully passed through to US importers, $300-800/household annually
White House already spent $12B on farmer bailouts; soybean prices at 10-year lows
Consumer sentiment strong at 100; dollar stable — no imminent domestic crisis
G20 Osaka summit (late June) provides natural negotiation venue
Remaining $300B tariff list would disproportionately hit US consumer products

Trump signs Executive Order 13873 (securing information/communications technology supply chains). Commerce moves to restrict Huawei.

Wall Street suffers worst day since January. Dow down 617 points (2.4%). Trump promises aid for farmers. Soybean prices hit 10-year low. White House already paid out $12B in aid.
U.S. Commerce Department adding Huawei Technologies and 70 affiliates to Entity List, making it much more difficult to buy parts from U.S. companies.
Latest US charges could knock 0.5 percentage points off annual Chinese economic growth. Loss could widen to 1 percentage point if both sides extend penalties to all exports.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Announce our already-planned retaliatory tariff increases on $60B of US goods as scheduled, but keep the response proportional and avoid escalatory rhetoric. Signal through state media and back-channels that we remain willing to negotiate, targeting the G20 Osaka summit (late June) as the next opportunity for leaders to meet. Do NOT dump Treasurys or take other financial-nuclear options. Restrict rare earth export discussions to aspirational policy signals, not concrete action yet.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high but not existential. Three converging pressures drive my +0.55 threat score:

(a) Tariff escalation is accelerating: List 3 rose from 10% to 25% on May 10, covering $250B of Chinese exports, and USTR has initiated process for 25% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B (timeline entry 2019-05-05, 2019-05-10). If enacted, this would cover virtually all Chinese exports to the US — our largest single-country export market.

(b) The Huawei Entity List action (EO 13873, signed May 15) represents a qualitative escalation beyond tariffs into technology containment. Adding Huawei and 70 affiliates to the Commerce Entity List threatens our most globally competitive tech firm and signals the US is willing to weaponize supply chains, not just impose tariffs. This directly threatens Made in China 2025 ambitions.

(c) Our retaliatory capacity is structurally constrained. China imports far less from the US (~$120B) than it exports (~$540B), meaning we are running out of US goods to tariff. Our $60B retaliation list (announced May 13) is already near the ceiling of what we can target. Reuters analysis (May 15) confirms China is 'running out of options to hit back without hurting its own interests.'

However, several factors prevent me from scoring this as existential (+0.8 or higher): Q1 2019 GDP came in at 6.4% — beating expectations and matching Q4 2018 — with industrial production surging 8.5% in March, the strongest since July 2014 (CNBC, SCMP, April 17). Our stimulus measures (record 8.2T yuan in Q1 credit) are working. The $300B tariff is in public comment phase with a June 17 hearing, buying time. And the US is not unscathed: US 10-year yields have fallen 69bp (3.06→2.37%), consumer sentiment data shows fragility, and US farmers are hurting from our agricultural retaliation.

The action_score of -0.3 (mild retaliation) reflects the need to demonstrate resolve — domestically and to the US — without triggering a further spiral. We must retaliate proportionally to maintain credibility (we promised 'necessary countermeasures'), but our limited retaliatory toolkit and strong Q1 data mean we can afford to be disciplined. Escalating aggressively risks triggering the $300B tariff before the G20, while conceding now would signal weakness and invite further demands on structural issues (IP, subsidies, SOEs) that strike at our development model. The optimal strategy is calibrated retaliation plus quiet negotiation channels, aiming for a Trump-Xi meeting at Osaka.

G20 Osaka summit as potential off-ramp for Trump-Xi meeting
Yuan depreciation near 7.0 psychological threshold — risk of capital flight if weaponized
